I-01.method: The full join keeps items from either cart, including items with no match. Duplicate items produce every matching pair.
I-01.edgeDescription: Only A appears once, with cart2 set to NULL.

I-02.method: The result has one row per employee reachable from the CEO, who starts at depth zero. The path check prevents cycles. Employees disconnected from the CEO are excluded.
I-02.edgeDescription: Adding an employee whose manager is missing leaves the full result unchanged.

I-03.method: There is one row per employee and calendar year, which serves as the fiscal year. Pay is stored in whole cents. The primary key prevents duplicate rows for an employee and year, and constraints validate dates and pay. Missing years would need a separate check.
I-03.edgeDescription: The constraints reject a duplicate employee and year, a start date within the year, negative pay, and a NULL ID.

I-04.method: Each row is a TX order from a customer with at least one CA order. EXISTS checks for a match without duplicating the TX orders.
I-04.edgeDescription: Adding another CA order for the same customer leaves the full result unchanged.

I-05.method: Conditional aggregation produces one row per customer. If a customer has multiple numbers of the same type, the query takes the lexicographically greatest one. A real application would need an agreed rule for choosing a number.
I-05.edgeDescription: For a customer with only a Home number, Cellular and Work remain NULL.

I-06.method: A workflow is partially complete when the number of non-NULL completion dates is above zero and below the total number of steps. Using COUNT for both also meets the bonus requirement.
I-06.edgeDescription: Adding a workflow with no completed steps leaves the full result unchanged.

I-07.method: Each row is a candidate who has all the required skills. The query uses relational division, so a repeated requirement does not change who qualifies.
I-07.edgeDescription: Adding a duplicate requirement leaves the full result unchanged.

I-08.method: Each row summarizes one workflow by adding three binary flags. A missing flag leaves the total unknown.
I-08.edgeDescription: Three positive flags give Passed a value of 3.

I-09.method: Each row represents an ordered pair of employees with identical license sets. The query checks the set difference in both directions.
I-09.edgeDescription: Adding a duplicate license leaves the full result unchanged.

I-10.method: The summary row contains a non-integer mean where applicable, the median, the mode, and the range. If several values tie for the mode, the smallest wins.
I-10.edge: DELETE FROM t1; INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1),(2),(3),(4);
I-10.edgeDescription: For 1, 2, 3, and 4, the mean and median are 2.5, the selected mode is 1, and the range is 3.

I-11.method: Each row is a permutation without repetition. The inputs must be distinct and contain no commas. The permutation length comes from the data.
I-11.edgeDescription: Adding D gives 24 distinct permutations of 4 elements each.

I-12.method: For each workflow, the query averages the intervals between consecutive events and truncates the result to match the source. A workflow with one event has no interval to average.
I-12.edgeDescription: A workflow with just one event returns NULL for the average interval.

I-13.method: The balance starts at zero and adds one adjustment at a time. The ROWS frame follows the date and uses rowid to order movements on the same day. An explicit MovementID would be a better tie-breaker in production.
I-13.edgeDescription: With a second adjustment of -10 after +75 on July 2, the balances are 100, 175, 165, 15, 65, and -35.

I-14.method: The query returns one status per workflow. If all statuses agree, it keeps that status. A mix that includes an error is indeterminate. Otherwise, the workflow is running. The input statuses are non-NULL.
I-14.edge: INSERT INTO t1 VALUES ('Foxtrot',1,'Error'); INSERT INTO t1 VALUES ('Foxtrot',2,'Running');
I-14.edgeDescription: A mix of Error and Running returns Indeterminate.

I-15.method: The query joins the fragments into one row in Sequence order. The sequence key must be unique.
I-15.edgeDescription: The new fragment appears at the end, separated by a space.

I-16.method: The query puts the two endpoints in a canonical order, then sums the scores for each unordered pair.
I-16.edgeDescription: Adding the reversed pair increases the total by 10 without creating a new pair.

I-17.method: The query expands positive integer quantities into one row per unit. Zero quantities produce no rows.
I-17.edgeDescription: Adding an item with quantity zero leaves the full result unchanged.

I-18.method: The query reports the ranges of missing seats, the total missing between seat 1 and the highest seat number, and the counts of occupied even and odd seats.
I-18.edgeDescription: After occupying seat 1, the first gap is 2 through 6. There are 37 missing seats and 10 occupied odd seats.

I-19.method: A running maximum of end dates allows the query to merge overlapping intervals, including nested ones. Adjacent intervals stay separate if they do not overlap.
I-19.edgeDescription: Adding an interval already covered by an existing one leaves the full result unchanged.

I-20.method: The query selects the latest price for each product as of 2018-12-31, the reference date used to reproduce the source. When dates tie, rowid breaks the tie.
I-20.edgeDescription: Adding a price dated after the reference date leaves the full result unchanged.

I-21.method: A state qualifies when every customer has an average of monthly averages above 100. Months without orders are excluded. This accounts for the expected TX result even though some months for customer 1001 average exactly 100.
I-21.edgeDescription: Adding a TX customer with an average of zero excludes the state.

I-22.method: The query counts occurrences of each message by workflow and returns all workflows tied for the highest count for that message.
I-22.edgeDescription: When Alpha and Tie match for Status Complete, both appear.

I-23.method: Each player goes into one of two balanced groups. If the total is odd, the first half gets the extra player. The ID breaks score ties.
I-23.edgeDescription: Six players split three per half. Players with equal scores are ordered by ID.

I-24.method: The page contains orders at positions 5 through 10 after sorting by the unique OrderID. Those positions can differ from the ID values.
I-24.edgeDescription: Removing the first order shifts the page to IDs 6 through 11.

I-25.method: For each customer, the query selects the suppliers with the most orders. Each order counts once regardless of the quantity in Count. Ties are retained.
I-25.edgeDescription: When both suppliers have two orders for customer 1001, both appear.

I-26.method: One row summarizes 2018 and the two preceding years. Each column sums all sales for that year and shows zero if the year has no sales.
I-26.edgeDescription: Adding a sale in 2015 leaves all three totals unchanged.

I-27.method: The delete removes duplicate values and keeps the row with the smallest rowid for each value. Running it a second time leaves the table unchanged.
I-27.edgeDescription: Adding another copy of an existing value before deletion leaves the same distinct result.

I-28.method: For each position, the query uses the current value if known or carries forward the last known value before it.
I-28.edgeDescription: An initial NULL remains NULL because there is no earlier value to carry forward.

I-29.method: Each row describes a run of adjacent, equal states in StepNumber order. A gap in step numbering does not break a run.
I-29.edgeDescription: Adding Failed after Passed starts a fourth run with one step.

I-30.method: This SQLite adaptation uses a view with a sentinel column that raises an error when SELECT * reads it. Explicitly named columns remain readable. The runner registers forbid_star(). The sentinel demonstrates query behavior and does not provide access control.
I-30.edgeDescription: Selecting the two columns explicitly succeeds. SELECT * raises Explicit columns required.

I-31.method: Three queries find the second distinct value. DENSE_RANK handles repeated salaries. With fewer than two distinct values, the aggregate returns NULL and the other queries return no rows. In the salary bonus, 150000 ranks second even when both top ranks have ties.
I-31.edgeDescription: Adding another copy of the highest value leaves the full result unchanged.

I-32.method: Each profession gets the IDs with the highest and lowest mission counts. The lower ID wins a tie.
I-32.edgeDescription: Adding a tied employee with a larger ID leaves the full result unchanged.

I-33.method: For each order, the slowest production task determines the time needed because the tasks run in parallel. Assembly is assumed to add no time.
I-33.edgeDescription: When the time needed equals the maximum, the order is On Schedule.

I-34.method: The query excludes the combination of customer 1001 and amount 50. The IS NOT conditions keep rows with NULL values that do not match that combination.
I-34.edgeDescription: A row with a NULL customer and amount 50 stays in the result.

I-35.method: The result has one row per representative who sold in exactly one category. Multiple sales in that category count as one category.
I-35.edgeDescription: Adding another sale in the same category leaves the full result unchanged.

I-36.method: Each row is a simple route from Austin to Des Moines. The visited path prevents cycles and repeated cities. The fixture has a minimum route cost of 500 and a maximum of 600.
I-36.edgeDescription: Adding a link back to Austin leaves the full result unchanged because it would repeat a city.

I-37.method: The query gives each order the rank of its three-attribute combination. The numeric keys depend on the combinations in the current dataset.
I-37.edgeDescription: An added row with the same combination receives key 1.

I-38.method: The report has one row per region and distributor, with total sales or zero. There are no dates in the fixture, so the report covers one implicit period.
I-38.edgeDescription: An extra sale raises the ACE/North total to 15. There are still 12 pairs.

I-39.method: Each row is a prime number. The query tests possible divisors up to the square root and excludes 1 and negative numbers.
I-39.edgeDescription: Adding 49 leaves the full result unchanged because 7 divides it.

I-40.method: The query lists cities in the specified order. Cities outside that list come last, sorted alphabetically.
I-40.edgeDescription: Boston is outside the specified list and appears last.

I-41.method: The query returns one row per node in the undirected graph. The smallest name identifies each connected component. UNION discards repeated visits and lets the recursion finish even if the graph contains a cycle.
I-41.edgeDescription: Adding another connection within the same component leaves the full result unchanged.

I-42.method: Each row is a friendship stored in a canonical order. The query counts neighbors shared by both people in the undirected graph. Duplicate friendships are ignored.
I-42.edgeDescription: Adding the same friendship in reverse order leaves the full result unchanged.

I-43.method: Each order shows the running minimum for its customer. OrderID must be unique within a customer so the window has a consistent order.
I-43.edgeDescription: A new minimum of 1 for customer 1001 changes only that customer's window.

I-44.method: Each customer version covers an inclusive date range. The start dates must be unique for each customer. A version ends the day before the next one begins, and the latest version stays open.
I-44.edgeDescription: A customer with a single version gets 9999-12-31 as its end date.

I-45.method: The query selects the earlier version when its inclusive interval overlaps the start of a later one. Selecting only the earlier version follows the source convention.
I-45.edgeDescription: Adding a non-overlapping version leaves the full result unchanged.

I-46.method: Both formulations return accounts that never had a positive balance. Zero is allowed. A NULL balance excludes the account because its history is unknown.
I-46.edgeDescription: Both formulations accept an account with a single balance of zero.

I-47.method: Each row is a segment between shift and activity boundaries. The intervals are half-open, and activities are clipped to the shift. If activities overlap, the lower rowid wins so the duration is counted once.
I-47.edgeDescription: Shift B has no activities, so it returns one Work segment of 120 minutes.

I-48.method: A salesperson qualifies by making at least one sale in each of the three years. The reference year is fixed at 2021 to match the source independently of the current date.
I-48.edgeDescription: Adding 2019 for salesperson 2002 leaves 2002 and 4004 qualified.

I-49.method: The query returns the last person in the queue whose running weight total is at most 2000. All weights are positive and people cannot be skipped.
I-49.edge: UPDATE t1 SET weight=2001 WHERE line_order=1;
I-49.edgeDescription: If the first athlete exceeds the limit, nobody enters.

I-50.method: Each valid pitch produces a row. The recursive state tracks balls and strikes, and a foul cannot add a strike beyond two. The sequence ends at four balls, three strikes, or a ball in play.
I-50.edgeDescription: Adding a pitch after the turn ends leaves the full result unchanged.

I-51.method: The SQLite adaptation registers SHA-256 and CRC32 in the runner in place of HASHBYTES and CHECKSUM. It hashes a canonical JSON array that distinguishes NULL from strings. CRC32 differs from SQL Server's CHECKSUM and does not guarantee uniqueness. A hash does not replace a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key.
I-51.edgeDescription: NULL is serialized unambiguously. The SHA-256 value is 64 hexadecimal characters long.

I-52.method: Each customer gets one row. CHECK enforces the length and the exact positions of ASCII digits. NOT NULL requires a phone number.
I-52.edgeDescription: The constraints reject a short number, letters in digit positions, an extra digit, and NULL.

I-53.method: Each row represents one person. The query ranks reciprocal pairs by the lexicographically larger member, matching the GroupID convention in the source.

I-54.method: The result is one row with the total payout. A ticket pays 100 if it contains all winning numbers or 10 if it contains some of them.
I-54.edgeDescription: Adding a non-winning number to a ticket leaves the full result unchanged.

I-55.method: Each product name is unique within its table. The full join distinguishes missing products from differences in quantity. The query treats two NULL quantities as equal.
I-55.edge: INSERT INTO t1 VALUES ('Null',NULL); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES ('Null',NULL);
I-55.edgeDescription: A product with NULL quantities in both tables is marked as a match.

I-56.method: The recursion returns one integer per row from 1 through 10. The recursive step has an explicit stopping condition.
I-56.edgeDescription: Creating an unrelated table still gives the same ten consecutive rows.

I-57.method: The query returns one token per row, with positions starting at 1. The semicolon stays in the token. Consecutive spaces produce explicit empty tokens.
I-57.edgeDescription: Two spaces between A and B produce an empty token.

I-58.method: The recursive parser evaluates one integer expression per row. It handles digits, plus, and minus without executing the text as code. Spaces and parentheses are outside its input domain.

I-59.method: The query removes adjacent matching pairs until nothing changes. An empty remainder means the string is balanced. Order matters even when the counts of opening and closing brackets agree. The worst case is quadratic.
I-59.edgeDescription: The crossed brackets ([)] are unbalanced even though the counts match.

I-60.method: A code appears if it is linked to exactly one distinct product. Codes stay as text to preserve leading zeros.
I-60.edgeDescription: Adding a duplicate association for the same product leaves the full result unchanged.

I-61.method: Each attempt is compared with the first and final scores. The source assigns a flag of 1 to the first attempt. To count as an overall improvement, every increase must be strictly positive.
I-61.edgeDescription: When the final score matches the previous one, the overall flag for 1001 is 0.

I-62.method: Each car and boat pair must differ in price by at least 200000. The expected output treats the source wording “200000 more” as an inclusive threshold.
I-62.edgeDescription: The Lamborghini priced at 290000 matches the boat priced at 90000 because the difference is exactly 200000.

I-63.method: An order qualifies when it contains exactly one product and every row has the PROMO discount. Duplicate rows are allowed. A NULL discount fails the check.
I-63.edgeDescription: Adding a NULL discount excludes order 3.

I-64.method: The query checks each string for exactly two quotation marks and more than 10 characters between them. It returns Error when there is only one quote, a case the source leaves open.
I-64.edgeDescription: Exactly ten characters between quotes returns False.

I-65.method: Each New Listing or Relisted event gets a new global key. Later events for the same home inherit it even if other homes have events in between. An event without an earlier opening has a NULL group.
I-65.edge: INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (10,'Home A','Pending'); INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (11,'Home C','Relisted');
I-65.edgeDescription: With interleaved events, Home A stays in group 2 and Relisted starts group 6 for Home C.

I-66.method: Each row is a kit. Components are ordered by date and serial number and matched by FIFO position within their types. Missing parts appear as NULL.
I-66.edgeDescription: The last kit remains in the result with Nut set to NULL.

I-67.method: The query groups people by their full date of birth, including the year. It returns shared dates with the names sorted alphabetically.
I-67.edgeDescription: Adding a unique date of birth leaves the full result unchanged.

I-68.method: For each team, the query removes the score furthest from its original average. A tie goes to the earliest year. The new average is truncated to match the source. A team with just one score has no remaining average.
I-68.edgeDescription: Adding a team with only one observation leaves the full result unchanged.

I-69.method: Each row gives a node and its main branch. The root appears in every group. The groups follow the order of the root's children, and UNION limits duplication.
I-69.edgeDescription: H is a child of E and belongs to branch 1.

I-70.method: Each family gets a row with the difference between the oldest and youngest ages and the largest gap between consecutive ages. Genders follow age and ID order. The mean is truncated to match the source, and a single child gives zero age gaps.
I-70.edgeDescription: For an only child aged 10, the mean is 10 and all gaps are zero.

I-71.method: Each row represents a hire. The runner enables foreign keys. Symmetric triggers prevent an employee from appearing in both tables, including through UPDATE. SQLite serializes writes.
I-71.edgeDescription: The test rejects six operations: duplicate membership, orphan inserts on both sides, and cross-table updates in both directions.

I-72.method: Each repair renews the warranty. Repairs are sorted by date and ID, and a repair qualifies when it follows the previous one by at most 30 days. A gap over 30 days starts a new sequence.
I-72.edgeDescription: A repair exactly 30 days later qualifies and is the first covered repair in its sequence.

I-73.method: For each step, the query counts the distinct statuses seen in the same workflow up to and including that step. COUNT DISTINCT ignores NULL.
I-73.edgeDescription: A repeated status does not increase the distinct count.

I-74.method: The query pairs adjacent players in the rankings. It sorts scores in descending order, breaks ties by name, and puts each pair's names in alphabetical order.
I-74.edgeDescription: Adding a league with a single player leaves the full result unchanged.

I-75.method: The query sorts each box's three dimensions to give equivalent rotations the same group. It assumes positive, non-NULL dimensions.
I-75.edgeDescription: A rotated version of A or B stays in group 1.

I-76.method: Each row marks the beginning of a batch. The first GO on or after that row ends the batch. When GO is missing, the end is NULL. The query examines the statements without executing them.
I-76.edgeDescription: A batch without GO has a NULL end.

I-77.method: For each NULL reading, the query uses the larger of the nearest known readings on either side. It uses the single available neighbor at a boundary and leaves NULL if both neighbors are missing.
I-77.edgeDescription: An initial NULL takes the only available neighbor, 52.

I-78.method: The query returns one row per status if the codes table is non-empty. EXISTS checks for any match without multiplying the rows.
I-78.edgeDescription: An empty codes table yields no status rows.

II-01.method: The query returns each integer from 1 through n and its factorial. Results are exact through 20! in a signed 64-bit SQLite integer. Larger values require arbitrary-precision integers.
II-01.edgeDescription: With n=1, the result is a single row (1,1).

II-02.method: Each row is a permutation of the integers from 1 through n. A bitmask prevents repeated elements. The number of rows grows factorially, so this approach is practical for small n.
II-02.edgeDescription: With n=1, the only permutation is 1.

II-03.method: The query returns each growing prefix of the integers from 1 through n. It uses text to preserve the concatenated values.
II-03.edgeDescription: With n=1, the only prefix is the text value 1.

II-04.method: Each row is a permutation in which adjacent values do not differ by 1. Using n=4 reproduces the two expected rows. The description uses n=10 as an example.
II-04.edgeDescription: There are no valid permutations for n=3.

II-05.method: Each row chooses concatenation, addition, or subtraction between the digits from 1 through n. The supported range is n=1 through 9, with 3^(n-1) combinations. The query builds the sum without evaluating the expression as code.
II-05.edgeDescription: With n=1 there are no operators, and the value is 1.

II-06.method: Each row is a binary string of length n. Text preserves leading zeros.
II-06.edgeDescription: Length zero produces one empty string.

II-07.method: Each row is an ordered selection of k distinct values from 1 through n. The recursion stops after k selections. The base fixture gives 24 triples.
II-07.edgeDescription: With n=3 and k=2, all six ordered pairs appear without repeats.

II-08.method: Positions 1 through 4 are the drivers of the motorcycle, sidecar, golf cart, and car. Position 5 is the sidecar passenger, 6 and 7 are golf cart passengers, and 8 through 10 are car passengers. People 1 through 5 are adults and 6 through 10 are children. Ordering passengers within each vehicle avoids duplicate arrangements. There are 120 driver choices and 60 passenger assignments per choice, for 7,200 arrangements.
II-08.edgeDescription: Three adults cannot drive four vehicles, so no arrangements qualify.

II-09.method: Each token has a starting position, the position of the next space, and the total number of spaces. The next space is NULL for the last token. The source removes the final token's semicolon.
II-09.edgeDescription: ONE yields one token with no following space and zero spaces overall.

II-10.method: The query reports the ranges of missing seats, the total missing between seat 1 and the highest seat number, and the counts of occupied even and odd seats.
II-10.edgeDescription: After occupying seat 1, the first gap is 2 through 6. There are 37 missing seats and 10 occupied odd seats.

II-11.method: Each row describes a run of adjacent, equal states in StepNumber order. A gap in step numbering does not break a run.
II-11.edgeDescription: Adding Failed after Passed starts a fourth run with one step.

II-12.method: The query returns one row per generated number. It doubles when the result would be below 100, then adds 1 at a time. The source gives no endpoint, so the setup uses a limit of 110.
II-12.edgeDescription: With a limit of 1, only the seed value appears.

II-13.method: The query returns C(row,col) with zero-based indices. The integer multiplication formula gives C(5,2)=10 and is subject to signed 64-bit overflow.

II-14.method: The query returns the survivor of the Josephus problem. With n=7, it starts counting at person 1, counts that person, and eliminates every third person. It converts the zero-based recurrence to a one-based answer.
II-14.edgeDescription: With just one person, the survivor is 1.

II-15.method: The deck contains 52 cards with four suits and ranks 2 through 14. Each of the 51 prediction rows compares the counts of higher and lower cards remaining. A seeded draw breaks ties. Drawing the same rank counts as a loss.
II-15.edgeDescription: With seed 42, an independent JavaScript implementation checks the 52 unique cards, the remaining counts, and all 51 predictions.

II-16.method: One row summarizes 10,000 trials, including wins for staying and switching and the count of invalid openings. The host knows where the prize is and opens a door with a goat. Switching has a theoretical win probability of about 2/3, which the simulation estimates.
II-16.edgeDescription: In a single trial, exactly one strategy wins and the host opens a valid door.

II-17.method: The summary counts completed games and reports the average, minimum, and maximum number of physical rolls. Under the chosen interpretation, a 6 starts penalty rolls, and each penalty roll subtracts its face value. Another 6 keeps the penalty active. The score cannot fall below zero, and every game must finish before the 10,000-roll limit.
II-17.edgeDescription: At a target of 1 over 100 games, an independent JavaScript simulation using the same draws confirms the average, minimum, and maximum. No game reaches the cutoff.

II-18.method: The summary counts how many of 10,000 groups of 23 share a birthday and reports the frequency. Birthdays are independent and uniformly distributed over 365 days, with no leap days or seasonal effects. The theoretical probability is about 0.5073.
II-18.edgeDescription: With one person in each group, none of the 100 trials has a shared birthday.

II-19.method: Each row gives a possible winner and the observed frequency over 10,000 circular random walks. The host at position 0 starts as visited. A trial stops when one position remains unvisited. The test checks the step limit, and the seven eligible participants have roughly equal chances.
II-19.edgeDescription: With two people, the only non-host participant wins all 100 trials.

II-20.method: One row summarizes a 100,000-day chain with the total days, rainy days, and the rainy fraction. The first day is sunny. The chance of rain the next day is 0.5 after sun and 0.7 after rain. The theoretical stationary fraction is 5/8, or 0.625.
II-20.edgeDescription: A one-day chain starts sunny and has zero rainy days.

II-21.method: The query runs 10,000 permutations of 100 boxes and reports trials, successes, success frequency, and the maximum number of decomposition steps. Each prisoner follows the cycle of their own label. All succeed if no cycle is longer than 50. The theoretical probability is about 0.3118. The outcomes are dependent, so 0.5^100 does not apply.
II-21.edgeDescription: With four prisoners and 100 trials, an independent JavaScript cycle decomposition verifies the result exactly with a two-box limit.

II-22.method: Each row describes a partition with the maximum number of groups for an order. Each group has one or two items and a cost of at least 10. Bitmasks keep groups disjoint, and items may go unused. Enumeration is exponential and uses integer row IDs from 1 through 62. Order 5 has one group per solution in the expected table, although the source comment says two.
II-22.edgeDescription: An order with a single item costing 9 has zero qualifying groups and a NULL combination.

II-23.method: The query tries all eight L-shaped offsets from 4D and returns one row per legal move. Both coordinates must stay within 1 through 8. The exercise asks for the next move, so the query stops after one jump.
II-23.edgeDescription: From corner 1A, the only legal moves are 2C and 3B.
